Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Newport/Morehead City NC
709 AM EDT Sat Aug 22 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
The Flood Watch has been cancelled early.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1) Increased risk of thunderstorms with heavy rainfall 
continues today

2) Drier air and a reduced risk of thunderstorms Sunday and 
Monday, especially inland. A thunderstorm risk may linger along 
the coast.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...A mid-level shortwave will lift slowly 
northeast along the coast of the Carolinas this morning, then 
shift away from the coast this afternoon. An attendant area of 
low pressure will also lift northeast along the coast while 
pulling a warm front north with it. The SFC low and warm front 
are expected to provide an area of enhanced low-level 
convergence along their trek up the coast. How close to the 
coast the low travels, and how much instability can be realized,
will be important factors for which areas see the heaviest 
rainfall rates today. Given how convectively overturned the 
airmass is from yesterday, it may be that the instability 
gradient will reside right along the immediate coast, which 
would favor areas from coastal Onslow northeast through the OBX 
for the heaviest rainfall today. It's also possible that the 
instability gradient remains just offshore, keeping the higher 
rainfall rates offshore as well. Regardless, the heaviest 
rainfall axis should reside east of where the heaviest rainfall 
axis was yesterday, and east of where the Flood Watch originally
covered. In light of that, the Flood Watch has been cancelled, 
and a watch is not currently anticipated for the coastal areas 
today due to 1) sandy soils which can be harder to flood, and 2)
uncertainty regarding whether or not the higher instability 
will develop along the coast or offshore.

Further inland, showers and scattered thunderstorms remain 
possible, but rainfall rates should be lower than yesterday due 
to less instability. However, some instances of minor poor 
drainage flooding may still occur. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...An anomalously strong upper level trough is 
forecast to translate east from the Great Lakes to the Northeast
U.S. Sunday and Monday. Meanwhile, an associated strong cold 
front is forecast to push east across the Mid-Atlantic and 
Carolinas with much drier air in tow behind it. Normally this 
would spell a reduced risk of thunderstorms for ENC, and for 
most areas it probably will. However, recent guidance has 
started to trend slower with the front's eastward progression as
the upper level forcing shifts NE away from the region, leaving
the tail end of the front to potentially stall near the coast 
of the Carolinas. There appears to be 2 possible scenarios at 
this point, each of which is outlined below.

SCENARIO 1: The front clears the coast of ENC. This scenario 
favors a reduced risk of convection areawide along with slightly
below normal overnight lows and lower humidity. This scenario 
was previously favored, but has recently lost some model 
support. 

SCENARIO 2: The front makes it to the coast, but then stalls. 
In this scenario, dry conditions are favored inland, but with a 
risk of thunderstorms lingering along the coast. Interestingly, 
this scenario offers the potential for a sneaky strong to severe
thunderstorm risk as drier mid-level air becomes more 
supportive of damaging downbursts. Lift and shear could also be 
enhanced as the area would remain in the entrance region of a 
strong upper jet. Lift could also be enhanced if a surface low 
rides up along the stalled front. Machine learning guidance do 
not show much of a signal for strong to severe convection, while
the ECMWF's EFI guidance does show a decent signal. This 
scenario has been gaining some support in recent runs. 

For now, much of ENC is likely to remain dry Sunday and Monday,
but for coastal areas, the thunderstorm risk is something worth
keeping an eye on.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Forecast confidence is low to moderate over the next 24 hours. 

An area of low pressure will lift northeast along the coast of 
North Carolina this morning, then move away from the area by 
this afternoon. Inland of the low, the TAF sites will have to 
contend with periods of IFR/MVFR, with brief bouts of LIFR 
conditions possible this morning. Eventually, CIGs should rise 
to high end MVFR or VFR levels. Low CIGs or BR/FG may redevelop 
tonight, but confidence in this is low. 

A risk of TSRA will accompany today's low as well, although the
greatest risk looks to be focused along, and just inland of, 
the coast. TSRA will be capable of LIFR/IFR VIS and gusty winds 
to 40kt.

Outlook: A stronger cold front is forecast to reach the area on
Sunday, but guidance now suggests it may stall along the coast 
through Monday. Should this occur, the TSRA risk would linger 
along the coast longer than previously forecast. However, even 
in that scenario, the risk may remain just east of the TAF 
sites.

&&

.MARINE...
Low pressure will lift northeast along the coast of the 
Carolinas this morning, then shift away from the area this 
afternoon. There will be an increased risk of thunderstorms 
along this low, especially for the central and southern waters. 
The inland rivers and sound and the northern coastal waters will
still have a risk of thunderstorms today, but the risk looks a 
bit lower compared to yesterday. The low is not particularly 
strong, therefore winds should remain below 25kt for most 
waters. The exception is the outer coastal waters where 
occasional gusts to 25kt can be expected where the gradient will
be the strongest. For the nearshore coastal waters, seas of 
2-3ft are expected through tonight. For the outer coastal 
waters, seas of 3-5ft are expected.

Outlook: A strong cold front will move into the ENC waters on 
Sunday, but may stall over the area through Monday. Where the 
front stalls is where the thunderstorm risk will be the highest 
through Monday. Strong winds of 40kt+ and waterspouts will be 
possible with the strongest storms. Eventually the front is 
forecast to move away from the area with winds laying down. Seas
of 2-4ft are expected through Monday, but then are expected to 
lay down to around 2ft by Tuesday.
